title: Instilling an Active Mind in Avatars via Cognitive Simulation
one_liner: To make avatars truly expressive, combine an AI reasoner that understands emotion and intent with a diffusion model that fuses audio, images, and text into natural motion.
lead: Video avatars today can move smoothly but often feel robotic because they just sync motion to audio waves without understanding what the character is actually trying to express. This paper proposes two ideas working together: first, an AI reasoner (like a brain) that reads the audio and images to figure out the character's emotion and intent, and second, a specialized diffusion model (a method for gradually building images by removing noise) that accurately blends audio, images, and text guidance to produce motion that feels authentic and emotionally coherent.

paras: Current video avatar generators work by taking audio and images of a person and then generating new video frames showing smooth motion. The problem is they treat audio like a simple mechanical signal—they learn to sync lips to the loudness and pitch of sound waves, nothing more. They never actually understand what emotion the person is expressing (sadness, excitement, confusion) or what intent drives the motion (asking a question, making a point, showing surprise).

A beginner might try to fix this by just adding more training examples or making the model bigger. But that does not work because the audio signal alone does not carry emotional meaning—it carries only raw frequency patterns. Without something to interpret those patterns and figure out intent, no amount of data helps, because the model has no way to learn the connection between an ambiguous audio signal and a specific emotion. It is like learning to recognize whether someone is excited or nervous just from their voice—without seeing their face or knowing the context, these sound nearly identical, so pure audio-based learning is stuck. The motion stays robotically tied to the audio waveform instead of reflecting the character's inner mental state.

callout.html: Before generating motion, use an AI reasoner to read the audio and images and figure out what emotion and intent are happening, then feed that understanding to a specialized motion generator that fuses all the information together.

steps.text: A language model reads the audio transcript and images to infer emotion, intent, and context.
The language model outputs a structured text description (for example: 'character is confused, tilts head, asks a clarifying question').

A specialized diffusion model receives three input streams: audio (encoded as a list of numbers), image features, and text (encoded as a list of numbers), all mixed together in a neural network layer.
During training, the model learns from both the first and last frame of the video clip, preventing the static reference image from blocking motion learning.
The diffusion process gradually removes noise, using the semantic guidance and audio to sculpt motion that matches emotion and intent.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: Instead of feeding audio directly into the motion generator, the paper inserts a language model in front that reads the audio and images, figures out the character's emotion and intent, and outputs a text summary. This summary then flows into the motion generator alongside the audio and images. Because the text summary directly names the emotion and intent, the motion generator can learn to connect motion patterns to emotional meaning, rather than just to audio waveforms. This works because semantic text is unambiguous (the word 'excited' always means one thing) while audio is ambiguous (excitement and anxiety sound similar).

hidden.name: semantic alignment
paras: Semantic alignment is how well the generated motion matches the actual emotion and intent of the character, rather than just matching audio waveforms. For example, if someone says 'I am confused' in a sad tone, pure audio-driven motion might sync lips perfectly but move the head calmly—missing the confusion. Semantic alignment means the head tilts, the gaze shifts, and the hands gesture in ways that express confusion.

The paper measures semantic alignment through user studies where humans watch the video and rate whether the motion feels emotionally consistent with what the character is expressing. They also compute objective metrics like motion naturalness and gesture dynamics (how expressive the head and hand movements are). The agentic reasoning module directly improves this hidden quantity because it explicitly names the emotion and intent, which the diffusion model then uses as guidance.

heat.caption: Darker means higher semantic importance. Highlighted cells show where reasoning informs motion generation.

reads.html: Semantic alignment means the motion expresses what the character is actually feeling and trying to communicate, not just what the audio waveform suggests.

The language model reasoning generates a text summary of emotion and intent that the diffusion model uses to guide motion. This improves semantic motion naturalness (as evaluated by users watching the video and rating whether motion matches emotion) and gesture dynamics (how expressive the head and hand movements are) because the model now has explicit guidance about what to express instead of just audio signals.

paras: Emotion and intent live in a different layer of meaning than raw audio. Audio carries frequency patterns; emotion carries information about mental state. A diffusion model (a neural network that learns by watching videos) looking only at audio must guess mental state indirectly, which is hard—like trying to guess someone's mood just by listening to their voice without seeing their face or knowing what they are saying. Is a high pitch excitement or anger? Is fast speech enthusiasm or nervousness? These are ambiguous.

By adding a language model that can read both the audio transcript and the visual reference image, the system can answer these questions directly. The reasoner sees the person says 'This is amazing' and sees them smiling, so it infers excitement, not anxiety. This explicit semantic information then flows into the diffusion model as text (encoded as numbers), giving it a clear goal for what kind of emotion and intent to produce in the motion. The diffusion model can now focus on the harder problem: generating motion that looks natural and physically plausible while expressing that specific emotion. This works because the diffusion model no longer has to guess what the character is feeling—the semantic text tells it directly.

The paper also introduces a technical trick called pseudo last frame conditioning. During training, the model learns from both the first and last frame of the video sequence. This prevents the static reference image from blocking the learning of motion—when the model sees the ground truth last frame is different from the first, it learns that large motion is allowed and should be learned from the semantic guidance.

pseudo last frame prevents image blocking motion

math.h2: The diffusion equation with semantic guidance
math.words: At each denoising step, the model predicts which noise to remove from the motion. The prediction is guided by a weighted combination of audio, image, and text information. The final loss measures how well the predicted motion matches the ground truth video.
math.equation: L = E[ ||x_0 - x_pred||^2 + lambda_sem * sem_guidance_loss + lambda_audio * audio_consistency_loss ]
symbols: the model's predicted clean motion after noise removal
weight for how strongly semantic guidance influences the result
penalty if the generated motion contradicts the semantic intent
penalty if lip sync is poor

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scenario: video clip with character saying 'I am excited' and the LLM inferred 'excited + forward lean'.
At a denoising step, the diffusion model has two choices for the head: stay vertical or tilt forward.
Baseline loss (prediction error): tilt forward is 0.5 units off ground truth; stay vertical is 0.4 units off ground truth.
Semantic guidance adds a penalty: staying vertical contradicts 'excited' intent, so add 0.3 units to the vertical choice.
New effective loss: tilt forward is 0.5, stay vertical is 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7.
The model chooses tilt forward because it now has lower loss, bringing the motion into alignment with the semantic intent.

math.note: The diffusion model is nudged by semantic guidance to prefer motion that matches emotion and intent, not just motion that is close to some baseline prediction.

bars.h2: Comparison: audio-only versus audio plus semantic guidance

charts.title: Audio-only method (reactive)
charts.note: Syncs well to audio but motion feels mechanical because there is no understanding of intent.

charts.title: With agentic reasoning (reactive + deliberative)
charts.note: Adds semantic understanding so motion is both accurate and emotionally coherent.

items.html: If the agentic reasoner misunderstands the audio (for example, mistakes sarcasm for sincerity), the semantic guidance will be wrong and the generated motion will express the wrong emotion. The motion will look natural but mean the opposite of what was intended.

If the semantic text says 'excited' but the audio is quiet and measured, the diffusion model must resolve the conflict. Poor weighting of lambda_sem versus lambda_audio can lead to motion that is jarring or incoherent.

With multiple people in one video, audio and semantic guidance can become ambiguous (who is speaking? whose emotion?). The method requires speaker-specific masking to keep audio features tied to the correct person.

When the LLM correctly infers intent, and the multimodal diffusion model weights semantic guidance appropriately relative to audio and image, the result is motion that is both lip-synced and emotionally coherent.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a video avatar generator that takes an audio clip, a reference image of a person, and text describing the emotion (for example, 'excited', 'confused', 'angry'). Generate a short video clip of the character performing an action in that emotional state. Measure three things: (1) how well lips sync to audio, (2) how much the motion changes when you change the emotion text (if emotion text is ignored, the output will be identical regardless of input), and (3) have humans rate whether the motion feels emotionally consistent.
demo.closing: The demo succeeds if motion naturalness and emotional consistency improve when semantic guidance is added, even if lip sync stays equally good. This works because semantic text is unambiguous (the word 'excited' clearly means one emotion) while audio is ambiguous (excitement and anxiety sound similar), so the semantic text helps the model learn what motion matches what emotion more clearly than audio alone can.
